notes.meaning: A fool here is not someone who lacks intelligence, but someone who chooses to ignore God. In his inner thoughts, he lives as though God does not see or judge his actions. This deep rejection of God leads to a spoiled life and wicked deeds.

The Lord is pictured bending down from heaven like a judge examining the human race. He looks closely to see if anyone shows true spiritual wisdom by seeking Him. True understanding always begins with honoring God and asking for His help.
God finds that humanity has turned away from His good path. People have become morally spoiled, like milk that has gone sour. Left to themselves, no one does pure good in God's eyes.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some ancient Greek and Latin copies of the psalm add six more lines after this verse, the same ones Paul uses in Romans 3:13-18. Many scholars think these lines were copied into the psalm from Romans, though they were read in churches very early.

notes.meaning: God asks if evildoers have lost all sense. They crush and exploit God's humble people as easily and thoughtlessly as eating their daily bread. Along with their cruelty, they refuse to pray or acknowledge the Lord.

Sudden terror overtakes these wicked oppressors, even when they think they are completely safe. Their guilty consciences make them tremble before God's judgment. They realize with fear that God is present to defend His faithful people.

Sinners try to mock and ruin the hope of the poor. The poor man's only plan is to rely completely on God, which the proud view as foolish. Yet that trust is safe, because the Lord Himself is his secure refuge.

David cries out for God to send complete deliverance from Zion, where the Lord sits enthroned. He looks forward to the day God rescues His people from distress and reverses their losses. When the Lord brings this restoration, all Israel will erupt in joy.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars think this verse, or even the whole psalm, comes from the time when Israel was in exile in Babylon. They read it as a prayer for the captives to return home.
